NEW DELHI: The Brics bloc on Saturday agreed on a joint declaration that it is "unlikely to name any country but will condemn unilateral war by any country," Reuters reported, citing four sources.The agreement comes as leaders of the 11-member grouping gather in New Delhi for the annual Brics summit this weekend.Member countries have been working to bridge differences between Iran and the United Arab Emirates, which are on opposite sides of the Gulf conflict, to reach consensus on the declaration, the sources said.The leaders are expected to approve the declaration on Saturday, according to the sources.India is hosting the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability".The summit reflects India's focus on strengthening cooperation among member countries and addressing shared priorities, with leaders expected to discuss major global and regional developments.The Brics grouping comprises Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.The bloc's partner countries are Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.India began its fourth Brics chairship on January 1, having previously chaired the grouping in 2012, 2016 and 2021. The year 2026 also marks 20 years since Brics was established.
Article Summary: The agreement comes as leaders of the 11-member grouping gather in New Delhi for the annual Brics summit this weekend. The leaders are expected to approve the declaration on Saturday, according to the sources. Article Title: Malaysia, Ethiopia for stronger defence cooperation with India as PM meets leaders

NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi met his Malaysian and Ethiopian counterparts, Anwar Ibrahim and Abiy Ahmad Ali, on the sidelines of the BRICS summit on Saturday. Government sources said that meetings resulted in taking India’s relations with both countries on a new trajectory, as Malaysia and Ethiopia expressed their keenness for stronger defence cooperation with India.Joint personnel training as well as defence procurement from India was discussed, according to Indian officials. “Both countries welcomed Indian industry and Investment.Ethiopia welcomed Indian mining companies. Opportunities in the semiconductor industry were discussed with Malaysia,” said a source.According to an official readout, Modi and Ibrahim took stock of the outcomes of Modi’s visit to Malaysia in February 2026 and reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation across a range of areas, including trade and investment, defence and security, semiconductors, infrastructure, digital economy, energy, fintech, education, tourism and people-to-people ties. Ibrahim conveyed Malaysia’s concurrence to the establishment of Consulate General of India in Kota Kinabalu, Sabah.“Prime Minister Modi appreciated Malaysia’s continued support in strengthening ASEAN-India relations. The leaders exchanged views on key regional and global issues of mutual interest. They expressed their continued commitment to advancing the India-Malaysia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership,” said the Indian readout.In the meeting with the Ethiopian PM, the leaders discussed further strengthening the bilateral Strategic Partnership. They reviewed progress across key sectors, including economic cooperation, defence and security partnership, and capacity building. The meeting built on Prime Minister Modi’s historic visit to Addis Ababa in December 2025, said an Indian readout.The two leaders also exchanged perspectives on regional and international developments of mutual interest and reaffirmed their commitment to close cooperation in multilateral fora, according to Indian officials.“Prime Minister Modi expressed appreciation for Ethiopia’s participation in the 18th BRICS Summit and noted that its presence helped in reinforcing the collective voice of the Global South,” said the readout.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi held separate bilateral meetings with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in New Delhi on Saturday, with India seeking to deepen cooperation with both countries in defence, investment and emerging sectors.Sources said the talks with Ethiopia and Malaysia marked a new trajectory in India's relations with the two countries. Both expressed interest in strengthening defence cooperation with India, including joint personnel training and defence procurement, the sources said.The two countries also welcomed greater participation by Indian industry and investment. Ethiopia, in particular, expressed interest in Indian mining companies, while discussions with Malaysia covered opportunities in the semiconductor sector, according to the sources. PM Modi met Anwar on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Leaders' Summit, where Malaysia is participating as a BRICS partner country at India's invitation. The Malaysian prime minister is scheduled to deliver a national statement on "Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth" at the summit.According to Malaysia's Foreign Ministry, the country is expected to push for stronger cooperation among BRICS members and partner countries on development challenges, economic opportunities and ensuring more inclusive access to technological advances and innovation.Anwar is also scheduled to visit Kerala, with the visit aimed at strengthening bilateral ties and expanding cooperation in areas including trade and investment, the digital economy, talent and labour, education and regional connectivity.PM Modi also met Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed at Hyderabad House. Ethiopia joined BRICS as a full member in January 2024, alongside Egypt, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.The latest talks build on growing India-Ethiopia defence engagement. Earlier this month, officials from the two countries discussed ways to expand cooperation in military training, defence industry collaboration and UN peacekeeping. The discussions also covered new and emerging areas of defence cooperation.The ministry of defence had said after the meeting between Ethiopian Charge d'Affaires Nebiyu Tedla and Defence Ministry Joint Secretary Amitabh Prasad that the two sides discussed "avenues to further strengthen India-Ethiopia defence cooperation, including training, defence industry collaboration and UN Peacekeeping, with focus on new and emerging areas."

India seeking to deepen cooperation with both countries in defence, investment and emerging sectors. Both expressed interest in strengthening defence cooperation with India.

Article Title: Xi Jinping in Delhi after 7 years: China talks 'fairness, justice', cites Brics' 'enormous potential'
Article Text:
China’s Xi heads to Brics summit with proposals to deepen Global South cooperation.

Xi expected to outline China’s priorities

China to lead Brics in 2027

Chinese president Xi Jinping landed in New Delhi for the 18th Brics summit, where he will hold talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and present Beijing’s proposals for greater cooperation among Global South countries.Ahead of the meeting, China’s state-run Global Times described Brics as an increasingly important platform at a time of global uncertainty. In an editorial, the Chinese government mouthpiece said the grouping’s strength came from its commitment to openness, cooperation and fairness."The key lies in its commitment to openness and inclusiveness, its goal of win-win cooperation and its pursuit of fairness and justice. The more turbulent and transformative the world becomes, the more the unique value of Brics cooperation comes into focus. As greater Brics cooperation enters a stage of improving quality and efficiency, there is growing confidence that Brics cooperation has enormous potential and that the future of Brics countries is bright. "Xi is expected to exchange views with other leaders on the international situation, the future development of Brics and ways to deepen practical cooperation.The newspaper said Xi would also put forward China’s initiatives for expanding and improving cooperation within the grouping."Since 2013, President Xi has put forward a series of important proposals and initiatives, including the "Brics Plus" cooperation model, driving the rapid development of Brics cooperation and enabling it to deliver greater results, while playing a pivotal role at every critical juncture in the mechanism's development."The editorial also highlighted China’s support for the New Development Bank, the expansion of Brics and cooperation in areas such as peace, innovation, green development and people-to-people exchanges."From advocating the Brics Spirit of "openness, inclusiveness and win-win cooperation" to proposing the concept of the "Brics Plus" cooperation model; from championing the establishment of the New Development Bank in Shanghai to supporting the historic expansion of Brics and proposing to build a Brics committed to peace, innovation, green development, justice and closer people-to-people exchanges, China has actively worked to strengthen and expand Brics cooperation, continuously improved the mechanism in line with changing times and steadily enhanced its global influence, earning broad recognition from all sides," the editorial adds.China will take over the rotating Brics presidency in 2027. The Global Times said Beijing would use the term to strengthen unity through multilateralism and align development strategies among member countries.It said China would also promote its Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative, Global Civilization Initiative and Global Governance Initiative. The newspaper identified the digital economy, green development, artificial intelligence, poverty reduction and agriculture as areas where China would seek concrete outcomes.The editorial concluded, "A 'Greater Brics' that is more united, efficient, pragmatic and committed to shouldering its responsibilities will surely open up new space for the common development of the Global South and inject greater certainty and positive energy into a world beset by turbulence and change."India is hosting the 18th Brics summit under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”. The agenda focuses on development, sustainability, innovation and strengthening the grouping as a constructive forum for the Global South.
Article Summary: China’s state-run Global Times described Brics as an increasingly important platform at a time of global uncertainty. China will take over the rotating Brics presidency in 2027. The Global Times said Beijing would use the term to strengthen unity through multilateralism and align development strategies among member countries.

Article Title: China Southern to resume Guangzhou-Delhi flights after 6 years ahead of Xi's Brics visit
Article Text:
Air connectivity between India and China has gradually improved in recent months.

Direct air links between India and China return

Xi leaves for Brics summit

China Southern Airlines will restart regular passenger flights between Guangzhou and New Delhi from September 21, the Global Times reported on Saturday.The announcement came ahead of Chinese president Xi Jinping’s visit to India for the Brics summit. The airline said the resumption would take its total operations across eight round-trip routes in South Asia to more than 100 flights a week. The Guangzhou-New Delhi service had been suspended for six years.Air connectivity between India and China has gradually improved in recent months.Air China resumed its Beijing-Delhi service in April, while China Eastern Airlines restarted direct flights between Kunming and Kolkata on April 18.Indian carrier IndiGo also launched a daily non-stop service between Kolkata and Shanghai on March 30. The airline had earlier restored flights from Kolkata to Guangzhou and later began operating from Delhi to the Chinese city.The resumption of direct flights followed confirmation from India’s ministry of external affairs. Air links between the two countries had been suspended during the Covid-19 pandemic and amid tensions following the Doklam and Galwan standoffs.Xi left Beijing on Saturday for the 18th Brics summit in New Delhi at Modi’s invitation, China’s state news agency Xinhua reported.The Chinese president is scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi later in the day.Xi’s delegation includes Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China and director of its General Office, and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi.According to Xinhua, Xi is expected to advance proposals on cooperation among Global South countries, building on his remarks at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek.Brics has become a major platform for emerging economies to coordinate on trade, finance, technology, development and global governance. The grouping also seeks to promote greater cooperation among countries of the Global South.
Article Summary: China Southern Airlines will restart regular passenger flights between Guangzhou and New Delhi from September 21. Announcement comes ahead of Chinese president Xi Jinping’s visit to India for the Brics summit. Air links between the two countries had been suspended during the Covid-19 pandemic and amid tensions following the Doklam and Galwan standoffs.

Article Title: Tamil Nadu govt tells staff to file annual asset declarations online by October
Article Text:

CHENNAI: Tamil Nadu govt has made it mandatory for all govt employees, barring All India Service officers, to submit their annual statements of assets and liabilities online through the Integrated Financial and Human Resources Management System (IFHRMS).The move follows an amendment to Rule 7(3) of Tamil Nadu Government Servants’ Conduct Rules made in Jan 2026 by the DMK regime. Employees are required to declare their immovable properties, including land and buildings, movable assets such as vehicles, jewellery and bank deposits, as well as debts and other liabilities through the IFHRMS portal. “The facility for filing details of assets and liabilities has now been enabled on the IFHRMS portal. The system will make it easier to monitor violations,,” a senior official said.In a recent communication, the govt directed secretaries, heads of departments, district collectors, judges, TNPSC secretary and registrar of Madras high court to instruct employees to file statements for the calendar year ending Dec 31, 2025, by Oct 31, 2026.The date of filing will be recorded in an employee’s ‘annual confidential report’.Failure to submit the statement within the stipulated period will be treated as a violation of the service conduct rules.Employees must file statements of their assets and liabilities as on Dec 31 of each year by March 31 of the succeeding year. The govt has also advised employees to keep their IFHRMS user IDs and passwords secure. Employees have to use Form I for immovable property, Form II for movable property and Form III for debts and other liabilities. After verifying and correcting the details, they must confirm and submit the declaration and download a copy for their records.“Not many employees take the declaration seriously. Submission of the statement will be considered during panel preparation for promotion. Making it mandatory is a welcome step as it would help prevent corruption at all levels,” said a member of Jactto-Geo, an umbrella federation of govt employees.In July, the TVK govt introduced a WhatsApp number — 9498180936 — for reporting instances of govt employees demanding bribes. Heads of departments were directed to ensure that anti-bribery notice boards were prominently displayed in govt offices and public places.
Article Summary: The move follows an amendment to Rule 7(3) of Tamil Nadu Government Servants’ Conduct Rules made in Jan 2026 by the DMK regime. Employees are required to declare their immovable properties, including land and buildings, movable assets such as vehicles, jewellery and bank deposits.

Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Thursday paid floral tribute to the state's first chief minister and freedom fighter Pandit Govind Ballabh Pant on his 139th birth anniversary, recalling his contributions to India's freedom struggle, governance and social reforms.Speaking at an event held to mark the birth anniversary, Yogi Adityanath described Pant as a great advocate and the first chief minister of Uttar Pradesh in 1947, when present-day Uttarakhand was also part of the state."As the first chief minister of Uttar Pradesh... he initiated efforts to present the Article Title: Trump’s ‘deepest, darkest China’ gets a Brics sequel with Iran's cameo as India walks tightrope
Article Text:
PM Modi, Pezeshkian & Putin at Brics Summit 2026 (left); PM Modi, Xi and Putin at SCO summit in 2025 (right)

Trump pressure on Brics

India walks a tight rope

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What could be a fresh diplomatic headache for Donald Trump? A picture of Prime Minister Narendra Modi holding hands with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, with Russian President Vladimir Putin standing alongside them at the Brics Summit , has brought together three countries whose ties with Washington range from strategic competition to open confrontation.The image also echoes a remark Trump made last year after PM Modi, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping were pictured together at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit. “Looks like we’ve lost India and Russia to deepest, darkest, China. May they have a long and prosperous future together!” Trump had said.This time, Iran, one of Washington’s most adversarial rivals, has joined the picture, adding another layer to the geopolitical message from a grouping that Trump has repeatedly viewed with suspicion. The US president has not yet commented on the Brics summit.US President Donald Trump has repeatedly warned Brics against challenging the dominance of the US dollar, putting the grouping’s push for greater use of local currencies at the centre of tensions with Washington. In November 2024, Trump threatened 100% tariffs on Brics countries if they backed another currency to replace the dollar.“We require a commitment from these Countries that they will neither create a new Brics Currency, nor back any other currency to replace the mighty US Dollar or, they will face 100% Tariffs, and should expect to say goodbye to selling into the wonderful US economy,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.Trump has also dismissed the prospect of Brics replacing the dollar in global trade, saying there was “no chance” of that happening and warning that countries attempting to do so should “wave goodbye to America”.The issue remains central to Brics’ economic agenda, although the grouping has increasingly focused on making trade and payments in national currencies easier rather than creating a common currency. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, speaking at the Brics Business Forum, called for greater use of national currencies among members, along with mechanisms to manage currency risks and facilitate reciprocal settlements.“One of the most important steps is to expand the use of national currencies in trade among the members. This step must be accompanied by the establishment of the necessary instruments for managing currency risks and reciprocal settlements,” Pezeshkian said.He also argued that the existing financial system was vulnerable because of its concentration around a limited number of currencies and called for the New Development Bank to play a bigger role in financing infrastructure and energy projects through local currencies and other mechanisms.Putin, meanwhile, did not directly mention replacing the dollar at this year’s forum. Instead, he described a broader shift in the global economic order, with emerging economies becoming increasingly important.“Right now, the world is undergoing structural, deep, profound shifts. It is explained by the fact that the so-called old leaders which used to be the vanguard of economic growth in the second half of the 20th century, are being replaced by new engines of growth. When I say old, this is just a formality - all of us understand what we are talking about,” he said.For Washington, the concern is not simply whether Brics creates a new currency, but whether a larger share of global trade and financial transactions gradually moves away from the dollar.For India, the Brics summit comes at a sensitive point in its economic relationship with the US. The India-US trade deal is “more or less” finalised, with the two sides working on a framework for preferential market access before signing it at an appropriate time. A few issues remain under discussion.The talks come as Trump continues to step up pressure on India over its purchase of Russian oil. In 2025, he had warned of further tariff action and later imposed 50% tariffs on Indian goods, adding to the economic stakes for New Delhi as it seeks to deepen trade with the US.India is meanwhile pursuing multiple trade agreements to widen market access. It has signed nine trade agreements over the past five years covering economies with a combined GDP of $60 trillion, while talks with Chile are at an advanced stage and New Zealand has been targeted for an early rollout.The balancing act is also reflected in India’s broader trade priorities. Its total exports reached $863 billion in 2025-26, including $421 billion in services, with the government seeking to diversify services exports beyond IT and professional services and expand areas such as fintech and digital services.The conflict involving Iran and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz have added another layer to the equation. The waterway is a crucial route for global oil shipments, making stability in the Gulf directly relevant to India’s energy security, trade and the safety of Indian seafarers.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has repeatedly warned Brics against challenging the dominance of the US dollar. The grouping’s push for greater use of local currencies is at the centre of tensions with Washington. Trump has also dismissed the prospect of Brics replacing the dollar in global trade, saying there was ‘no chance’ of that happening.

Article Title: Elephant Madhuri now on her way to Kolhapur as Anant Ambani's Vantara vows continued medical care
Article Text: Madhuri, the elephant popularly known as Mahadevi in Kolhapur, will be allowed to return to the city after the High-Powered Committee (HPC) passed an order on September 9, Anant Ambani’s Vantara said in a statement on Thursday.According to Vantara, the HPC permitted Madhuri’s return after hearing the parties' claims, reviewing reports, and inspecting the facility at Nandani in Maharashtra. The order has laid down several conditions, including that Madhuri cannot be used in processions or for any other purpose.The elephant will also need round-the-clock care and a medical examination every fortnight, Vantara said.Madhuri was brought to Vantara in Jamnagar on July 30, 2025, in compliance with directions from the HPC, which the Bombay High Court and the Supreme Court upheld. Vantara said it had not sought her custody but had received and cared for her in accordance with the directions.The organisation said Madhuri’s health had stabilised after sustained veterinary care, but her chronic conditions still require supportive management and regular monitoring.As part of the transition, Vantara said it had helped arrange living conditions, veterinary infrastructure, medical equipment, medicines and other necessities at the Nandani facility. Its veterinarians will visit Madhuri in Kolhapur every fortnight to conduct her medical examination and submit reports to the competent authorities, as directed by the HPC.Vantara also said it had worked to improve the enclosure at Nandani within the available infrastructure. Further upgrades, it said, were currently restricted by town-planning constraints, including a road passing through land belonging to the trust.The organisation added that it would remain available to support future upgrades at the facility and would assist if directed by the courts or competent authorities.“Madhuri’s wellbeing remains Vantara’s first concern. Our commitment to her health, welfare and dignity does not depend on where she lives,” the statement said.
Article Summary: Madhuri, the elephant popularly known as Mahadevi in Kolhapur, will be allowed to return to the city. The High-Powered Committee (HPC) passed an order on September 9. The order has laid down several conditions, including that Madhuri cannot be used in processions or for any other purpose.

NEW DELHI: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Friday conducted searches at nine locations in Bihar, Haryana and Delhi in connection with an alleged bank fraud involving Ramnandi Hotels and Resorts Ltd (RHRL), Gaya. The searches were carried out under Section 17 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) at six locations in Gaya, two in Gurugram and one in New Delhi, officials said.RHRL is controlled by Akhouri Gopal and his sons, Nishant and Nitesh, according to officials. The ED action follows an investigation into the alleged diversion of loan funds and suspected attempts to move properties to prevent possible attachment.During the probe, the agency found that RHRL allegedly diverted Rs 58 crore out of the Rs 85 crore disbursed by a consortium of banks led by Central Bank of India. The loans were allegedly obtained on the basis of fake or forged project completion reports provided by the company's chartered accountant.The loan facilities were also backed by personal guarantees from Akhouri Gopal and his family members, officials said.The investigation has also flagged five properties that had been pledged or mortgaged with Tata Motors Ltd against outstanding dues of a related group entity. The properties were allegedly sold recently despite being pledged.According to the ED, the properties were sold at grossly undervalued prices, with the sale deeds showing the consideration as cash receipts. Some of the buyers are suspected to be benamis or proxies of Akhouri Gopal, officials said.The agency suspects the transactions were aimed at alienating the properties and preventing coercive action. Some of the buyers were reportedly people of modest means who may not have had the financial capacity to arrange the amounts involved in the transactions.The proceeds of crime in the case, based on the CBI chargesheet, are estimated at around Rs 131.79 crore, corresponding to the non-performing asset (NPA) value, officials said.The searches are part of the ED's ongoing investigation into the alleged bank fraud and related movement of assets.
Article Summary: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) conducted searches at nine locations in Bihar, Haryana and Delhi in connection with an alleged bank fraud. The searches were carried out under Section 17 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) Some of the buyers are suspected to be benamis or proxies of Akhouri Gopal.

NEW DELHI: India's Brics presidency has yielded over 50 tangible and practical outcomes, including frameworks and action plans, across the four priority pillars of resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability, official sources said ahead of the summit that begins Saturday.According to Indian authorities, the takeaways for India include an unequivocal condemnation of terrorism and commitment to combat it in all its forms and manifestations, along with a consensus for reform of institutions of global governance, strengthened multilateralism and support for India's UNSC membership bid.While there was still no clarity about the summit culminating in a unified declaration because of differences between UAE and Iran on the West Asia situation, govt sources said they were confident of a constructive outcome because of the support received by India's chairship.The foreign minister-level meeting had earlier ended without a consensual statement because of the discord over West Asia."With engagement spanning diverse sectors, 400 meetings during the year, India's chairship has demonstrated strong convening and consensus-building strength. The summit will begin with PM Narendra Modi chairing a session on strengthening multilateralism.Govt believes India has emerged as a bridge builder, positioning Brics as a platform for dialogue and constructive cooperation, as reflected in the consensus documents of ministerial/heads of agency meetings.According to govt, the presidency was a whole-of-nation effort, bringing together Centre, states, institutions, industry, academia, youth, civil society and communities, with events held in more than 30 cities."India's chairship has highlighted its rich heritage and culture, people-centric innovations, development experience and home-grown solutions as contributions to shared progress and cooperation," added an official.

Article Title: NMC adds over 13,000 MBBS seats, total intake tops 1.4 lakh
Article Text:
13,186 additional seats have been approved

NEW DELHI: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has approved 13,186 additional MBBS seats for the 2026-27 academic year, taking the total approved undergraduate medical intake to 1,40,214 seats across 836 medical colleges, excluding seats at the Institutes of National Importance (INIs).The updated seat matrix, as on September 1, incorporates permissions for new medical colleges and increases in the annual intake of existing medical colleges.The expansion comes as NEET-UG counselling for the 2026-27 MBBS batch is under way, with the counselling schedule pushing back the start of the academic session and subsequent rounds, including the stray vacancy round, expected to continue into Oct.The increase is heavily driven by the private sector, which accounts for 10,400 of the 13,186 additional seats, or nearly 79%, while govt medical colleges have added 2,786 seats. The total intake has risen from 1,27,028 renewed seats to 1,40,214, an increase of about 10.4%.Karnataka has recorded the highest increase with 1,650 additional seats; followed by Tamil Nadu with 1,250; Bihar with 1,240; Uttar Pradesh with 1,200 and Rajasthan with 1,100. Telangana has added 1,010 seats and West Bengal 975.Karnataka's total MBBS intake now stands at 15,745 seats, including 4,600 in govt colleges and 11,145 in private colleges.Tamil Nadu has 14,299 seats, Uttar Pradesh 14,400 and Maharashtra 13,249. The addition of 13,186 seats will widen the pool of MBBS seats available during the 2026-27 admission cycle, although the actual allocation of these seats will depend on the ongoing counselling process.Among other major increases, Andhra Pradesh has added 525 seats, Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand 520 each, Maharashtra 550, Haryana 350, Kerala 300, Gujarat 250, Puducherry and Uttarakhand 200 each, and Jammu and Kashmir 175.The NMC matrix shows zero increase in Delhi, while Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Dadra and Nagar Haveli have also recorded no additional seats.The NMC has made it clear that admissions must be restricted to the number of seats approved in the matrix, with admissions beyond the approved intake liable to regulatory action.
Article Summary: The expansion comes as NEET-UG counselling for the 2026-27 MBBS batch is under way. The increase is heavily driven by the private sector, which accounts for 10,400 of the 13,186 additional seats. The total intake has risen from 1,27,028 renewed seats to 1,40,214, an increase of about 10.4%.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court has directed FSSAI to spell out details of how front-of-pack food warning labels will look, their shape, size, colour, placement on packets and the timeline of implementation, leaving nothing to the discretion of the food regulator.The court also wanted to know how Centre plans to warn children about the dangers of junk food.After FSSAI agreed to implement labelling after being pushed by SC and filed an affidavit, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran put 13 questions to the regulator and gave 10 days' time for answers.Though SC acknowledged "significant progress" has been made by FSSAI on this issue of national importance, it said the regulator's affidavit was silent on various issues and several aspects of practical implementation required clarification.The 13 questions are part of the detailed order uploaded by the court on Friday, which also includes its observations from the previous day on why FSSAI proposed a two-phase rollout of the labelling requirements instead of implementing them in one go.According to FSSAI’s proposal, during Phase I, a red hexagonal warning would be placed on products high in two or more nutrients of concern, namely added fat, added sugar and salt, based on thresholds in the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024.The warning could carry declarations such as “HIGH FAT”, “HIGH SUGAR”, “HIGH SALT” and “HIGHLY SWEETENED BEVERAGE”. The proposed Phase II would extend the warning to products high in any one of the specified nutrients. The order questions the regulator on what basis it suggested the inclusion of food products high in “two or more” nutrients of concern and certain sweetened beverages in Phase I, and the inclusion of food products high in “any one” nutrient of concern in Phase II, respectively.The court also said sugar, salt and fat are called the “Unholy Trinity” and that “the ‘unholiness’ arises not only from the added sugar and added fat in a food product but the total value of these nutrients available in a product, which has to be considered.” The Supreme Court incorporated the suggestion of advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi that the threshold must be decided based on “total sugar” and “total fat” and not on the basis of “added sugar” and “added fat”. Referring to the 2021 FSSAI meeting, the Bench said, “It is clear from the aforesaid minutes that ‘total sugar’ and ‘saturated fat’ would be used for the purpose of the labelling. In this regard, we would like FSSAI to weigh in and indicate whether there has been a change in stance in comparison to the consensus arrived at in the aforesaid stakeholder consultation. If so, we would like to know how the underlying concerns are sought to be addressed.”The court also asked the regulator: “What are the dimensions of the ‘red hexagon’ proposed to be used in the FoPL (labelling)? Whether it would have standardised specifications or whether it would be calculated in proportion to the area of the package? Whether the font size used for FoPL would be relative to the dimensions of the hexagon themselves? The manner and method of the placement of such hexagon(s)?” It further asked, “Why has FSSAI suggested a combined/composite/singular hexagon for two or more nutrients of concern instead of separate/distinct/individual hexagons for each nutrient of concern?” The court posted the matter for hearing on September 28.
Article Summary: Supreme Court has directed FSSAI to spell out details of how front-of-pack food warning labels will look, their shape, size, colour, placement on packets and the timeline of implementation. Article Title: Counting Discounts
Article Text:
How good is that online deal? We’ll know from Jan 1

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For years, UK consumer group “Which?” has found that many Black Friday deals are not really bargains. A shop may say a product has been cut from £500 to £400, but the product may never have actually sold for £500. Last year, none of the deals checked by the group was the cheapest price that product had been sold for in the previous 12 months.You may have seen something similar during festive sales in India. A product you have been waiting to buy during a Diwali sale may suddenly become more expensive when the sale begins. The “discounted” price may even be the same as, or higher than, its earlier price.The good news is that this should change on e-commerce platforms in India from January 1. Under new rules, when a seller announces a discount, it will also have to show the product’s “prior price”. This means the lowest price at which the product was sold on that platform during the 30 days before the discount was announced.This gives shoppers a simple way to check whether a discount is real. Without such a rule, it is easy to be fooled when big sale signs and huge discounts create excitement.Other major markets already have similar protections. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission says a “former price” used in an advertisement must be a genuine price.California says it must have been the normal market price within the previous 90 days. The European Union introduced a similar rule in 2022, using a 30-day price history. Its rule also applies to shops, not just online sellers.India should do the same. Online shoppers can use price-tracking websites to check whether a deal is genuine. But if a shop puts a “60% off” sign on a shirt, there is no easy way to know whether it was really sold at the higher price before. A discount should be a real saving, not just a clever trick.
Article Summary: When a seller announces a discount, it will also have to show the product’s ‘prior price’ This means the lowest price at which the product was sold on that platform during the 30 days before the discount was announced. This gives shoppers a simple way to check whether a discount is real.

Article Title: 'Trade barriers rising globally, India building bridges': PM Modi at Brics business forum
Article Text:
Trade barriers rising globally, India building economic bridges: PM Modi at BRICS Business Forum

Brics is a grouping of 11 major economies.

Supply-chain resilience becomes a key priority

Infrastructure and strategic technologies

UPI as India's digital infrastructure model

Why Brics matters to India

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday positioned India as a bridge-builder in an increasingly fragmented global economy, saying the country is responding to rising trade barriers by expanding free-trade partnerships, strengthening supply chains and creating new avenues for businesses across the BRICS grouping.Addressing the Leaders' Session of the BRICS Business Forum in New Delhi, PM Modi said the global trading environment is becoming more difficult as countries increasingly turn to tariffs, restrictions and other barriers to protect domestic industries. Against this backdrop, he said, India is pursuing greater economic integration by negotiating and signing trade agreements with a growing number of countries.“Today, while trade barriers are rising globally, India is building economic bridges. Since 2014, we have entered into free trade agreements with nearly 40 countries,” PM Modi said.The Prime Minister's message was aimed not only at highlighting India's expanding trade network but also at presenting the country as a stable and increasingly attractive destination for investment at a time when global businesses are trying to reduce their dependence on concentrated supply chains.“Our approach remains focused on reducing barriers and expanding opportunities for businesses,” PM Modi said.PM Modi also used India's Brics presidency to push for greater economic cooperation among the 11-member grouping.Rather than limiting Brics cooperation to government-to-government engagement, India is seeking to create networks that allow companies, startups and smaller businesses to access new markets, investment and technology.Under India's chairship, new cooperation networks have been established in areas including agriculture, healthcare, skills development and smart grids. These initiatives are intended to translate the political and economic weight of BRICS into practical opportunities for businesses.India has also launched the Brics Incubator Network, Brics MSME Portal and Brics Startup Innovation Fund.These initiatives are particularly significant for startups and micro, small and medium enterprises, which often face greater difficulties than large corporations in entering overseas markets, finding investors and establishing business partnerships.“To connect startups and MSMEs with markets and finance, we have launched initiatives like the Brics Incubator Network, the Brics MSME Portal, and the Brics Startup Innovation Fund,” PM Modi said.He urged businesses from Brics countries to use these platforms to increase the movement of investment, technology and talent across member economies.A major theme of PM Modi's address was economic resilience. The disruption of global supply chains in recent years, from the Covid-19 pandemic to geopolitical conflicts and trade tensions, has pushed countries to diversify sources of energy, technology, raw materials and manufactured goods.India, PM Modi said, has been working to make its supply chains more diversified and reliable.“The theme of India's Brics chairmanship is 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability.' Over the past 12 years, India has made this mantra the foundation of its economic and trade policies,” he said.He pointed to India's efforts across sectors ranging from energy to technology, arguing that stronger and more diversified supply chains would help the economy withstand external shocks.“It is a result of this resilience that, even amidst global uncertainties, India today offers the assurance of growth and stability,” the PM said.The emphasis on resilience also reflects India's broader push to reduce vulnerabilities in strategically important sectors. The government has increasingly sought to build domestic manufacturing capacity while simultaneously attracting global companies looking to diversify production beyond existing manufacturing hubs.PM Modi highlighted infrastructure expansion as another pillar of India's economic strategy.India is rapidly expanding its network of roads, railways, ports and airports, he said, arguing that better physical connectivity is essential for lowering logistics costs and improving the movement of goods and people.At the same time, the government is trying to build domestic capabilities in technologies and industries that could have long-term economic and strategic importance.“We are rapidly expanding our roads, railways, ports, and airports. Simultaneously, we are building new capabilities in strategic sectors such as shipbuilding, semiconductors, quantum technology, critical minerals, and biotechnology,” PM Modi said.These sectors are increasingly important because they sit at the intersection of economic security and national security.Semiconductors, for example, are essential for everything from smartphones and automobiles to advanced weapons and artificial intelligence systems. Critical minerals are required for batteries, electronics and clean-energy technologies, while shipbuilding is important both for trade and maritime security.By expanding domestic capabilities in such areas, India is seeking to become not merely a large consumer market but a producer and supplier within global value chains.PM Modi also highlighted India's digital public infrastructure, particularly the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), as an example of how technology can expand economic participation.UPI has transformed the way payments are made in India by enabling fast digital transactions between bank accounts and mobile applications. PM Modi said the system has given fresh momentum to financial inclusion and digital payments on a massive scale.“Today, 50% of the world's real-time payments take place using this technology,” he said.India has increasingly sought to promote its digital infrastructure model internationally, particularly among developing economies. The broader objective is to demonstrate how digital systems can bring more people and businesses into the formal economy while making transactions faster and cheaper.The Brics Business Forum is the grouping's main private-sector platform, bringing together business leaders, government ministers and heads of state to discuss trade, investment, finance, technology and development.Its importance extends beyond discussions at individual meetings. Recommendations from the Brics Business Council and the Business Forum can feed into summit declarations and subsequent work programmes, giving the business community a role in shaping the bloc's economic agenda.The Leaders' Session in New Delhi was attended by Brics leaders, the Chairs of the Brics Business Council and the Brics Women's Business Alliance. Modi also joined the participating dignitaries for a group photograph.The forum is being held as India hosts the 18th Brics Summit under its 2026 chairship. India's presidency is centred on the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, with development, sustainability and innovation among its principal priorities.Brics has expanded considerably from its original five-member format and now comprises 11 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.Collectively, the grouping represents around 49.5% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade, according to background information on India's 2026 chairship.For India, the economic significance of Brics therefore goes beyond the traditional diplomatic role of the grouping. Its large consumer markets, energy producers, manufacturing economies and emerging technology sectors create opportunities for greater trade and investment.PM Modi's address sought to underline India's position within that changing economic landscape: as a country attempting to keep markets open, diversify supply chains, build strategic industrial capacity and use its digital infrastructure to expand economic participation.His broader pitch was that as geopolitical tensions and protectionism reshape global commerce, India wants to position itself as a reliable economic partner, one that can connect businesses, markets, investment and technology across an increasingly fragmented world.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi positioned India as a bridge-builder in an increasingly fragmented global economy. He said the country is responding to rising trade barriers by expanding free-trade partnerships. India has also launched the Brics Incubator Network, Brics MSME Portal and Brics Startup Innovation Fund.

So, can MPD-2047 be sustainable?

Can the city’s infrastructure keep pace?

By 2047, Delhi could be home to nearly 32 million people, need around 1,600 million gallons of potable water every day, generate nearly 26,000 tonnes of solid waste daily and require roughly 40 lakh additional homes.Those numbers tell a bigger story than population growth. They point to a city that will need to build more — while somehow using less land, less water and fewer resources, without compromising safety, mobility, liveability or the environment.That is the challenge at the heart of the Master Plan for Delhi 2047 (MPD-2047).The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) unveiled the MPD-2047 at the National Media Centre on August 20, 2026, presenting it as the fourth master plan for the capital, with a perspective extending to 2047. The authority has described the plan as a framework for shaping Delhi’s future growth, with its focus spanning housing, mobility, infrastructure, environmental sustainability and efficient land use.The plan comes after earlier master plans for 1962, 2001 and 2021. DDA’s current master-plan framework includes policies on transit-oriented development, land pooling, redevelopment of ageing neighbourhoods and ecological restoration, placing long-term urban growth alongside infrastructure capacity and sustainability.It envisions a denser, more connected and more transit-oriented Delhi, with large-scale housing, redevelopment of ageing neighbourhoods, stronger public transport, green-blue networks, ecological restoration and new approaches to land and infrastructure planning. It also pushes for compact growth, with development increasingly tied to the capacity of roads, public transport, water, drainage, sewerage and other essential services.But there is a larger question: Can Delhi grow at this scale without repeating the problems that already make the city struggle today?The question becomes harder to ignore when incidents such as the recent Satya Niketan building collapse enter the conversation. The tragedy exposed something the master plan itself acknowledges: planning a city is not enough if building safety, approvals, enforcement and infrastructure do not keep pace with growth.So, what does MPD-2047 promise, and can Delhi actually deliver it?Housing is perhaps the plan’s biggest promise. MPD-2047 estimates the city’s housing requirement at nearly 40 lakh dwelling units by 2047. The strategy combines affordable housing, rental housing, EWS housing, hostels and dormitories, affordable rental housing complexes and redevelopment of existing areas. The government says around 18 lakh affordable homes could come through transit-oriented development, while redevelopment of existing group and government housing could add around seven lakh dwelling units.Land pooling is another major pillar, with the DDA hoping to unlock large areas of land and potentially facilitate up to 20 lakh homes.This is sensible in a land-constrained city. But “affordable” is not simply a number of units. A home is affordable only if households can afford its purchase or rent, utilities, maintenance and commute.That makes displacement an important question. Redevelopment and densification can raise land values and change neighbourhood economics. The success of the housing strategy will therefore depend not only on how many homes are built, but who can actually continue to live in them.MPD-2047 also brings Delhi’s 357 villages into the larger redevelopment conversation. At a conference organised by the Dilli Dehat Project, speakers argued that the plan treats these villages primarily as areas for “regeneration”, rather than recognising them as historic settlements with distinct social, cultural and ecological assets. They also raised concerns about the protection of village commons such as ponds and grazing land, and the impact of road widening and land pooling on existing communities.MPD-2047 moves Delhi towards more compact development. It promotes redevelopment of brownfield areas, mixed-use development and transit-oriented growth, while encouraging higher intensity around mass-transit corridors. The plan also allows buildings of more than 100 floors to be developed as landmark projects in areas with adequate infrastructure.The idea is to support compact growth, reduce urban sprawl and free up more ground-level space for public and green areas. But density is not automatically sustainable.Concentrating growth near Metro and other mass-transit corridors can also make public transport more viable. Sustainability of vertical growth will depend on what surrounds these towers — transport, water, sewage, power, fire safety and open space. Building higher can save land, but only if infrastructure rises with it.Every additional floor brings additional demand for water, sewage, electricity, roads, parking, fire services, schools, healthcare and drainage. MPD-2047 itself takes an infrastructure-led approach: new development is intended to be supported by roads, public transport, water, sewerage, drainage, power and digital connectivity.The real test, therefore, is sequencing.Can infrastructure capacity be demonstrated before density is increased?That may be one of the most important implementation questions for MPD-2047.Water may be the plan’s clearest sustainability test.In 2021, Delhi’s water supply was about 935 MGD, against estimated demand of around 1,380 MGD. By 2047, potable-water demand is projected at approximately 1,600 MGD. The detailed augmentation calculation identifies about 401 MGD of additional supply, taking projected availability from roughly 1,000 MGD to about 1,401 MGD.That leaves an apparent gap of roughly 200 MGD against the 1,600 MGD demand estimate.The figures come from different stages and assumptions within the planning calculations, so they should not be treated as a simple supply-versus-demand failure. But they do highlight a genuine vulnerability: Delhi’s future growth cannot depend on finding water after development has already happened.That leaves an apparent gap of roughly 200 MGD against the 1,600 MGD demand estimate.The figures come from different stages and assumptions within the planning calculations, so they should not be treated as a simple supply-versus-demand failure. But they do highlight a genuine vulnerability: Delhi’s future growth cannot depend on finding water after development has already happened.That leaves an apparent gap of roughly 200 MGD against the 1,600 MGD demand estimate.The figures come from different stages and assumptions within the planning calculations, so they should not be treated as a simple supply-versus-demand failure. But they do highlight a genuine vulnerability: Delhi’s future growth cannot depend on finding water after development has already happened.Water recycling, rainwater harvesting, wastewater treatment, groundwater recharge and demand management therefore need to move from supporting provisions to core infrastructure.As MoHUA secretary D Thara recently told real-estate developers, housing projects need green areas, rainwater harvesting, water recycling and sewage-treatment infrastructure rather than simply buildings and roads.The Satya Niketan building collapse has put Delhi’s student housing and building-safety systems under scrutiny. A five-storey boys’ paying guest accommodation near Delhi University’s South Campus collapsed in September 2026, killing seven people, including five university students.The wider question is how safely Delhi’s high-density neighbourhoods are being managed. In Rajendra Nagar, severe waterlogging and drainage failures have repeatedly disrupted life, while the deaths of civil-services aspirants in a flooded coaching-centre basement in 2024 exposed serious gaps in building use, drainage and enforcement. Similar concerns have emerged around cramped PGs, narrow lanes and ageing buildings in student hubs.These incidents underline that urban growth is not only about adding housing and infrastructure. As MPD-2047 enables redevelopment and greater density, building permissions, structural safety, drainage, inspections and emergency access will have to keep pace.The real question is not how high Delhi can build, but how safely it can grow.Yes — the plan has the ingredients for a more sustainable Delhi: compact growth, transit-oriented development, affordable housing, green-blue infrastructure and infrastructure-led planning.But a plan is only a framework. Its success will depend on coordinated implementation, enforcement and infrastructure capacity.The key question is simple: Can Delhi build capacity as fast as it builds density?If yes, MPD-2047 could make Delhi more connected, resilient and resource-efficient. If not, it could simply make today’s problems bigger.The plan sets the direction. Delivery will determine the outcome.
Article Summary: The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) unveiled the MPD-2047 at the National Media Centre on August 20, 2026. It is the fourth master plan for the capital, with a perspective extending to 2047. It envisions a denser, more connected and more transit-oriented Delhi, with large-scale housing.

Article Title: TOI Social Impact Summit 2026: Conversations on technology , inclusion, resilience and community ownership
Article Text:
Technology can help bridge the education divide

Healthcare access remains unequal

Young people want a greater role in India's future

Inclusion must translate into ownership

Disaster management must move from response to resilience

AI must be an enabler, not a replacement

Communities must lead climate and environmental action

Building a city sustainably

A more inclusive approach to development

Disclaimer: This article is part of a brand initiative by TOI in partnership with Malabar Gold & Diamonds and Reliance Foundation.

The TOI Social Impact Summit 2026 examined how technology, AI, education, healthcare and community-led action can help create more equitable and resilient development.Technology can help bridge India's education divide, artificial intelligence must serve as an enabler, and inclusion must go beyond numerical targets, speakers said at the TOI Social Impact Summit 2026.The two-day summit brought together experts from education, healthcare, technology, civil society and business to explore how social-impact initiatives can become more accessible, locally relevant and sustainable.At the session on making education accessible, equitable and inclusive, panellists challenged the idea that technology is inherently elitist or exclusionary.Pranav Kothari, CEO of Educational Initiatives, said technology should not be seen as a replacement for teachers. Educators remain essential for inspiration, values, debates, experiments and project-based learning.However, technology can help address the continuity gap in education. While Indian schools operate for about few days a year and students attend school for roughly 140 days, digital tools can help learning continue throughout the year.B V R Mohan Reddy, Founder Chairman and Board Member of Cyient, said adaptive learning platforms could allow children to learn at their own pace instead of following classroom structures designed primarily for front-bench students.He cautioned against fear of artificial intelligence, saying the real divide in the future could be between those who understand and use AI and those who do not.Cyient adopted government schools, where the share of female students rose from 16-18% to 56%. Dropouts fell to about 2%, while the intervention also expanded to include AI labs, skilling and employment-linked training.Abdul Salam KP, Vice-Chairman of Malabar Gold & Diamonds, spoke about children from urban slums who remained out of school even after schools reopened following the Covid lockdowns.This led to the creation of slum micro-learning centres offering teachers, uniforms, books and meals. Children without documents were also assisted in entering the formal school system. The network has grown to around 2,500 centres serving approximately 1.2 lakh children every day.Gayatri Nair Lobo, CEO of Educate Girls, said enrolment was only the first step. Poverty, missing documents, domestic work, early marriage and the distance to secondary schools continue to push adolescent girls out of education.For every 100 primary schools in India, she said, there are only 20 senior secondary schools. Through open-schooling programmes, Educate Girls is helping young women return to education. One student who resumed her studies after a 10-year break went on to top the Class 10 examinations in Madhya Pradesh.The session on 'Health Equity and Access: Using Partnerships to Strengthen Primary Care' examined the continuing rural-urban gap in healthcare delivery.Dr Aparna Hegde, Founder and Managing Trustee of ARMMAN; Rizwan Koita, Chairperson of the Board, National Accreditation Board for Hospitals & Healthcare; Dr Shibu Vijayan, Chief Medical Officer – Global Health, Qure.ai; and Tushara Shankar, Head – CSR and Head of Lupin Foundation, Lupin Limited, participated in the discussion.Specialist care remains unevenly distributed, often forcing patients in underserved regions to travel long distances. The panellists highlighted the potential of partnerships, telemedicine, AI-led diagnostics and decentralised primary healthcare networks to improve access.The session on youth inclusion brought together Ariana Agarwal, Co-Founder and Product Lead, Plas-Stick; Kayden Anthony, Wildlife Biologist; Shubh Mehta, Co-Founder, Change is Us; and Unnathi Surana, UNICEF India Youth Advocate.The discussion examined how young people can participate more meaningfully in shaping India's corporate and social future.Surana articulated the expectations of young leaders:"Ten years from now, I don't just want to see more young people at a table. I want to see tables that were built differently because we were there."Panellists at the session on scaling inclusion argued that inclusion must go beyond numerical targets and quotas. It must give communities genuine ownership and representation.Chetna Sinha, Founder of Mann Deshi Bank & Foundation, shared the story of a rural woman named 'Nakusa', meaning 'Unwanted', who overcame extreme marginalisation and succeeded in getting her name recorded on 7/12 land extracts.Liby T Johnson, Executive Director of Gram Vikas, Odisha, cautioned corporations against imposing urban measures of success on rural women."Many women may prefer a modest but reliable income they can control rather than pursuing bigger enterprises," he said.Rachana Iyer, Head – CSR, IDFC FIRST Bank, spoke about programmes for marginalised groups, including rural women, people with disabilities and neurodivergent individuals.Rekha Pillai, Head – CSR, Castrol India, highlighted corporate-NGO partnerships that have supported more than six lakh people working in the unorganised sector.India is gradually moving from an approach focused only on disaster relief and emergency response towards mitigation and resilience, said Sudarshan Suchi, Chief Development Officer at Reliance Foundation.Speaking at the session on rebooting development for disaster resilience, Suchi said risk-informed planning could help reduce the impact of disasters while strengthening communities' ability to cope with and recover from natural hazards.Reliance Foundation's disaster management programme works across several states and increasingly focuses on community-led initiatives.Samhita R, Founding CEO of Resilience360, explained how artificial intelligence and large language models could provide quick, hyperlocal climate-risk assessments.Such tools, she said, could help communities and administrators make better decisions and build "future-proof communities."The session on 'Architecting Inclusive Futures: Navigating the Intersection of Tech, AI, and Social ESG Pillars' examined how technology can be adapted to local needs.Aniket Doegar, Co-Founder and CEO of Haqdarshak, spoke about using technology to help people access more than 20,000 government schemes and cash transfers. AI, he said, could address information asymmetry and simplify access to welfare benefits.Gautam Khanna, CEO of Maker Bhavan Foundation, highlighted innovation laboratories in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, where young engineers use AI to create, prototype, patent and commercialise physical products.Jyoti Sharma, CEO of Nasscom Foundation, and Richa Gautam, Director – CSR and Sustainability, Schneider Electric's Greater India Zone, emphasised that AI must supplement foundational technical skills and educators.S Senthilkumaran, Head – Platforms and Applications at Reliance Foundation, explained how AI was being used to convert Indian Meteorological Department weather updates into advisories in local languages and across formats including audio and video.AI can help teachers reach more students, panellists said, but should not make teachers irrelevant.The summit also featured a discussion on how corporates can support community-led initiatives for climate, water and environmental conservation.The session brought together Alok Mehta, Group Chief Governance Officer, InterGlobe Enterprises; Dr Geetanjoy Sahu, Professor and Dean, School of Habitat Studies, and Chairperson, Centre for Climate Change & Sustainability Studies, TISS; Kiran Sarkar, Head Sustainability – M&M Automotive & Farm Equipment Sector, Mahindra & Mahindra; Sangeeta Mamgain, Senior Core Team Member and Lead, School of Climate and Sustainability, Piramal Foundation; and Smitha Gopalakrishnan, Asia Sustainability Leader and India CSR Leader, 3M.The discussion placed community participation at the centre of climate and environmental action, while examining the role of corporate partnerships, sustainability leadership and local institutions in addressing water and ecological challenges.The session on 'Building a City Sustainably: Growth, Resilience and Liveability' featured Ashwini Bhide, Municipal Commissioner, BMC.Bhide underlined the importance of public participation in urban development."Participation does not mean that every citizen will decide whether a project will take place or how it should be executed. But it means making citizens feel that this is my city, this is my project," she said.Her observation reflected a larger theme running through the summit, that development is more effective and sustainable when communities feel a sense of ownership over the places and initiatives that affect their lives.Across the summit, speakers explored how innovation, partnerships and community-led action can come together to address some of India’s most pressing social challenges.From education and healthcare to climate resilience, youth participation, welfare access and urban development, the discussions underscored the importance of solutions that are inclusive, locally relevant and built to last.The summit highlighted a shift in how social impact must be approached, from delivering solutions for communities to creating solutions with them, with participation, ownership and accountability at the centre.
Article Summary: The TOI Social Impact Summit 2026 examined how technology, AI, education, healthcare and community-led action can help create more equitable and resilient development. The two-day summit brought together experts from education, Healthcare, technology, civil society and business to explore how social-impact initiatives can become more accessible and sustainable.

Article Title: TOI Social Impact Summit 2026: Piyush Goyal calls for low-cost innovations to drive social impact
Article Text:
At the

TOI Social Impact Summit 2026

, government and business leaders discussed responsible growth,

sustainable business models

, philanthropy, ESG and the role of capital markets in creating social impact.

Sustainability must be part of the business model

Fair practices are central to responsible enterprise

Making sustainability work for business

Can the Social Stock Exchange transform social impact?

Building a culture of giving

Gold and the circular economy

Disclaimer: This article is part of a brand initiative by TOI in partnership with Malabar Gold & Diamonds and Reliance Foundation.

India needs affordable, locally developed solutions to address some of its most pressing social and environmental challenges, Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal said at the TOI Social Impact Summit 2026.Calling upon startups and innovators to develop cost-effective and sustainable technologies, Goyal referred to an ongoing lake rejuvenation initiative in his North Mumbai parliamentary constituency. He said India needed locally developed solutions such as low-cost machines for cleaning and maintaining water bodies."Machines are internationally available but at a huge price. Maybe one of our startups will very easily be able to make it," he said.Reflecting on India's CSR framework, Goyal said he had initially believed that mandatory CSR spending could weaken the country's traditional culture of voluntary giving."When the Companies Bill was piloted about 13-14 years ago, bringing in the provision of mandatory 2% spend on CSR, we were in opposition," he said. "I had felt we were actually doing a disservice to the Indian ethos, to the Indian way of life, because in India people do not do CSR out of compulsion."However, he acknowledged that the policy had brought more funds into social development.Goyal also said government welfare initiatives, including affordable housing, had restored dignity, created household assets and helped expand the middle class. Rising dual-income households and improved living standards, he added, were also contributing to economic growth."This is a very profitable proposition when you serve society," he said.BCCL COO Mohit Jain added that national growth must be assessed not merely through output, investment and ambition, but through the lives strengthened by development."A tree does not grow upward alone but underneath as well. So it is with the nation," Jain said. "The true strength of a country is revealed at its roots — in the student who gains access to better education, the patient who receives timely care and the community that becomes resilient enough to face an uncertain future."ITC Chairman and Managing Director Sanjiv Puri said sustainability and inclusive growth must be embedded in the corporate sector's business model."Economic progress cannot be seen in isolation from sustainability. Both have to go together," Puri said. "Corporates must create economic value, because that creates the foundation to go beyond. But it must be both economic and societal value. And that is what we call responsible competitiveness."He urged organisations to look beyond short-term shareholder value, pointing out that responsible business behaviour was increasingly being demanded by regulators, global trade bodies and conscious stakeholders.Puri said the world was facing a "perfect storm" of geopolitical turmoil, the weaponisation of tariffs and the climate crisis. These pressures, he noted, were affecting livelihoods, food security and nutrition, with vulnerable communities facing the greatest threat.He called for closer cooperation between the government, corporate sector and civil society to address climate change and support India's low-carbon growth trajectory.Citing ITC's own business model, Puri explained how the company had developed an ecosystem involving specialised research and development, the cultivation of climate-resilient trees requiring less water for its paperboards business, and partnerships with small farmers for its fruit juices operations.He also said CSR must be treated as a long-term business venture, with measurable outcomes and strong community capacity."You have to first invest in building capacity at the community level so that the initiatives are sustained and built upon. Otherwise, over a period of time, they wither away," he said.Speaking at the inaugural session, MP Ahammed, Chairman of the Malabar Group, said ethical business practices, local compliance and transparency were central to responsible growth.Malabar Gold & Diamonds, founded in Kozhikode over three decades ago, operates across. Ahammed said the group's operations were aligned with the vision of "Make in India, Market to the World."He identified quality, warranty and guarantee as the three core principles guiding the company's business. He also described employees as the company's "biggest assets," particularly those involved in crafting its jewellery.Ahammed announced that the Malabar Group would allocate Rs 200 crore, or 5% of its net trading profit, towards CSR initiatives in 2026-27.The key focus areas will include education, hunger alleviation, healthcare and women's empowerment. Its 'Hunger Free World' initiative aims to provide food to vulnerable communities and contribute towards eliminating starvation.The summit also featured a discussion on how companies are integrating sustainability into their core strategy, operations and investment decisions to create long-term value for stakeholders.The session, titled 'Making Sustainability Work for Business, and Business Work for Sustainability', featured Dr Neha Garyali, Vice-President, Centre of Excellence, VeARC Technologies, and Prabodha Acharya, Chief Sustainability Officer, JSW Group.The discussion placed sustainability within the wider context of business strategy, rather than treating it as a separate or standalone corporate responsibility function.Another session examined the role of India's Social Stock Exchange in helping social enterprises access capital and improve accountability.The discussion, titled 'From CSR to Capital Markets: Can India's Social Stock Exchange Transform Social Impact?', featured Mangesh Wange, Chief Executive Officer and Board Member, Swades Foundation; Riddhesh Shah, Deputy Vice-President, BSE; and Vineet Shastry, Associate Vice-President, NSE.The session looked at the relationship between social impact, capital markets and institutional participation, while examining whether new financial mechanisms can help scale organisations working on social challenges.At the session on philanthropy, volunteerism and collective action, Sumit Tayal, CEO of Give, highlighted the changing culture of giving in India."It is assumed that people start to give when they have made a lot of money, but 18- to 25-year-olds are giving as much as people older than them. Women make up 50% of donors," Tayal said.The discussion focused on how philanthropy can become more participatory and collective, with younger donors, women and volunteers playing a greater role in supporting social causes.Gold, India's second-largest import commodity by value, is increasingly becoming part of the domestic circular economy.The session on 'Circular and Responsible Gold Value Chains: Unlocking Social and Environmental Impact' examined responsible sourcing, recycling, organised credit and the financialisation of gold.Asher O, Managing Director – India Operations, Malabar Gold & Diamonds, said the company meets around 80% of its demand through people trading in their old gold.Kaushlendra Sinha, CEO of the Indian Association for Gold Excellence and Standards, said younger buyers were increasingly seeking information about the source of gold and demanding proof of responsible sourcing.Sachin Jain, Regional CEO India, World Gold Council, said responsible mining in India could help reduce excessive dependence on imports.Mayank Sharma, President and Head of Gold Loan at IIFL Finance, discussed the role of gold loans in improving credit access for households and MSMEs. Vikram Dhawan, Head Commodities and Fund Manager at Nippon India Mutual Fund, spoke about the growing financialisation of gold through gold ETFs.Together, the discussions highlighted the need for greater transparency, responsible mining, recycling and organised financial systems across the gold value chain.
Article Summary: India needs affordable, locally developed solutions to address some of its most pressing social and environmental challenges, Piyush Goyal said. Government welfare initiatives, including affordable housing, had restored dignity, created household assets and helped expand the middle class. ITC Chairman and Managing Director Sanjiv Puri said sustainability and inclusive growth must be embedded in the corporate sector's business model.
